title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: Having returned to the regiment and told the commander about Denisov's situation, Rostov rode to Tilsit with the letter to the Emperor.
On the thirteenth of June, the French and Russian Emperors arrived in Tilsit. Boris Drubetskoy had asked the important personage he served to include him in the suite for the Tilsit visit.
"I'd like to see the great man," he said, referring to Napoleon — whom until now he, like everyone else, had always called Buonaparte.
"You are speaking of Buonaparte?" asked the general with a smile.
Boris looked at the general inquiringly and instantly realized he was being tested.
"I am speaking, Prince, of the Emperor Napoleon," he replied. The general patted him on the shoulder with a smile.
"You will go far," he said, and took him along to Tilsit.

Boris was among the few present on the banks of the Niemen on the day the two Emperors met. He saw the raft decorated with monograms, saw Napoleon pass before the French Guards on the far bank, saw the thoughtful face of Emperor Alexander as he sat silently in a tavern on the riverbank awaiting Napoleon's arrival, and watched both Emperors board their boats and meet on the raft — Napoleon stepping forward quickly to greet Alexander and extending his hand — before they both disappeared into the pavilion. Since entering the highest circles, Boris had made it his habit to observe everything carefully and note it down. At the time of the Tilsit meeting, he asked about the names and uniforms of Napoleon's entourage and listened closely to every word spoken by important people. When the Emperors entered the pavilion, he checked his watch and remembered to check it again when Alexander emerged. The meeting had lasted one hour and fifty-three minutes. He recorded this that same evening among other facts he considered historically significant. Since the Emperor's suite was very small, being present at Tilsit for this interview was a matter of great importance for anyone who valued his career. Boris, having secured this advantage, felt his position was now firmly established. He had not only become known — people had grown used to him and accepted him. Twice he had carried out missions for the Emperor himself, so that the sovereign knew his face, and everyone at court would have been surprised if he had been absent, rather than noticing his presence.

Boris was lodging with another aide-de-camp, the Polish Count Zhilinski. Zhilinski, a Pole raised in Paris, was rich, passionately pro-French, and nearly every day of their stay in Tilsit, French Guard officers and men from French headquarters dined and lunched with him and Boris.

On the evening of the twenty-fourth of June, Count Zhilinski arranged a supper for his French friends. The guest of honor was one of Napoleon's aides-de-camp; there were also several French Guard officers and a page of Napoleon's — a young man from an old aristocratic French family. That same day, Rostov — slipping into Tilsit in civilian clothes under cover of darkness to avoid being recognized — made his way to the quarters shared by Boris and Zhilinski.

Rostov, like the whole army he came from, was far from feeling the shift in attitude toward Napoleon and the French — enemies who had suddenly become friends — that had occurred at headquarters and in Boris's world. In the army, Bonaparte and the French were still regarded with a mix of anger, contempt, and fear. Just recently, talking with one of Platov's Cossack officers, Rostov had argued that if Napoleon were captured, he should be treated not as a sovereign but as a criminal. Quite recently, meeting a wounded French colonel on the road, Rostov had insisted heatedly that peace was impossible between a legitimate ruler and the criminal Bonaparte. He was therefore unpleasantly startled to find French officers in Boris's quarters, wearing uniforms he had only ever seen from the far side of the battle lines. The moment he glimpsed a French officer poking his head out the door, that combative hostility he always felt at the sight of the enemy seized him. He stopped at the threshold and asked in Russian whether Drubetskoy lived there. Boris, hearing an unfamiliar voice in the entry, came out to meet him. A flash of annoyance crossed his face when he first recognized Rostov.
"Ah, it's you? Very glad — very glad to see you," he said, however, coming toward him with a smile. But Rostov had caught his first reaction.
"I've come at a bad time, I think. I shouldn't have come, but I have business," he said coldly.
"No — I only wonder how you got away from your regiment. I'll be with you in a moment," he said, answering someone who called him.
"In a minute I shall be at your disposal."
"I see I'm intruding," Rostov repeated.

The look of annoyance had already vanished from Boris's face. Having apparently considered and decided how to handle things, he took both of Rostov's hands very calmly and led him into the next room. His eyes, looking steadily at Rostov, seemed somehow veiled — as if screened by blue spectacles of social propriety. So it seemed to Rostov.

"Oh, come now! As if you could come at a wrong time!" said Boris, and he led him into the room where the supper table was laid and introduced him to his guests, explaining that Rostov was not a civilian but a hussar officer and an old friend.
"Count Zhilinski — le Comte N.N. — le Capitaine S.S.," he said, naming the guests. Rostov looked at the Frenchmen with a scowl, bowed reluctantly, and said nothing.

Zhilinski clearly did not welcome this new Russian into his circle and didn't speak to Rostov. Boris seemed not to notice the strain the newcomer created, and with his usual pleasant composure and the same veiled look in his eyes, tried to keep the conversation going. One of the Frenchmen, with the characteristic politeness of his countrymen, addressed the stubbornly silent Rostov, suggesting he had probably come to Tilsit to see the Emperor.
"No — I came on business," Rostov replied curtly.

Rostov had been in a bad mood from the moment he noticed Boris's displeasure, and as always happens when one is out of sorts, everyone seemed to regard him with aversion and he felt in the way everywhere. And he really was in their way — he was the only one not taking part in the conversation, which had resumed. The glances his fellow guests cast at him seemed to say: "What's he doing here?" He stood up and went over to Boris.
"I'm in your way," he said quietly. "Come talk about my business, and I'll leave."
"Oh no, not at all," said Boris. "But if you're tired, come lie down in my room and rest."
"Yes, really..."

They went into the small room where Boris slept. Rostov, without sitting down, launched immediately — irritably, as if Boris were somehow to blame — into the story of Denisov's case, asking whether Boris could and would use his connections to intercede with the Emperor on Denisov's behalf and deliver the petition. Being alone with Boris, Rostov felt for the first time that he couldn't look him in the eye without discomfort. Boris, one leg crossed over the other, stroking the slender fingers of his right hand with his left, listened to Rostov the way a general listens to a subordinate's report — now looking aside, now gazing straight into Rostov's eyes with that same veiled expression. Each time this happened, Rostov felt awkward and dropped his gaze.

"I've heard of such cases, and I know His Majesty is very strict in these matters. I think it would be best not to bring it before the Emperor but to apply to the corps commander. But in general, I think..."
"So you don't want to do anything? Just say so!" Rostov almost shouted, not looking Boris in the face.
Boris smiled.
"On the contrary — I'll do what I can. Only I thought..."
At that moment Zhilinski's voice called Boris from the other room.

"Well, go then — go, go..." said Rostov, and declining supper, he stayed alone in the little room, pacing back and forth for a long time, listening to the lighthearted French conversation coming from next door.
